rv.q: This revival of the 1997 musical about conjoined twins and the vaudeville world that exploited them feels less like a resurrection than like major surgery that has left visible scars.
Side Show may never be a classic musical, but in this superb production it’s a hypnotic spectacle that packs an emotional wallop.
Condon created a big, old-fashioned, shamelessly entertaining musical that tells its human story while embracing issues beyond the showbiz saga.
The reimagined "Side Show" that opened Monday night at the St. James Theatre is a stunning, soaring, must-see musical.

Leading ladies Emily Padgett and Erin Davie are perfection as Daisy and Violet Hilton, conjoined twins in real life who were plucked out of a carnival midway by a rascal showman and transformed into vaudeville stars.
Yet this show also has a strange, slightly demented charm, especially in the vaudeville and carnival scenes.

The revival of 'Side Show' is a sumptuous production that showcases the considerable talents of Erin Davie and Emily Padgett as conjoined twins Daisy and Violet Hilton, but the musical itself remains a problematic work.
The problem with Side Show is that these stories can’t be separated, and only one can thrive.

The original production, which starred Alice Ripley and Emily Skinner, is not easily erased from memory...The piece has been revised for this Condon revival, which is a serviceable rendition of the main material with generally solid leading performances, but will, for die-hard fans, be something of a disappointment...
But while this sincere and stylishly designed production is perhaps the best that Side Show can be, that best, alas, isn’t great.
Condon shows musical-theater veterans how it’s supposed to be done.
But it does invite us to question the increasing nonchalance with which we dissect and ridicule public figures of all sorts.
But for the most part, Condon’s production is a stunning achievement and a must-see attraction for anyone who cares about serious, Sondheim-style musical theater.
The 2014 revival of Side Show is a marked improvement over the original 1997 production.
Still, there’s something amiss in this new “Side Show.”
We take a journey with these dreamgirls, but there's no truly satisfying payoff — or a portrait that goes deeper than the skin.
Certainly not this leaden, sporadically moving update—which bears little resemblance to the original production.
But it certainly doesn't work artistically.
Still, there is a great deal of talent prancing around on that stage, and you could do worse than share an evening enjoying them all.
